text: # My Study Notes: Automation, APIs and n8n These are notes I wrote for myself while learning automation and integration. I wrote them in simple words so they are easy to revise later. ## What is workflow automation? Workflow automation means letting software do repetitive tasks by itself. Instead of copying data from one app to another by hand, you build a workflow: a chain of steps where each step takes input, does something and passes the result on. A workflow has a trigger (what starts it), some actions in the middle, and an output at the end. ## n8n n8n is the workflow automation tool I use most. It is a visual, node-based tool. Each node is one step, such as receiving data, changing it, calling another service or sending a message. You connect nodes with lines, and the data flows from left to right. It is a great example of low-code work, because I can build useful automations quickly and only write a little code when I really need it. I like n8n because I can see the whole flow on one screen, test it node by node, and fix problems fast. ## Webhooks A webhook is a way for one app to tell another app that something happened, right when it happens. whole flow on one screen, test it node by node, and fix problems fast. ## Webhooks A webhook is a way for one app to tell another app that something happened, right when it happens. Instead of my workflow asking again and again "is there anything new?", the other app sends a message to a special URL as soon as there is something. In n8n, a webhook node gives me that URL, and the workflow starts whenever data arrives. It works like a doorbell: the workflow waits quietly and wakes up when someone rings. ## REST APIs and HTTP requests A REST API is a standard way for programs to talk to each other over the internet. I send an HTTP request to a URL, and the server sends a response back. The common request types are GET to read data, POST to send or create data, PUT to update and DELETE to remove. Requests often carry headers, such as an authorization key, and a body, and the answer usually comes back as JSON. ## JSON JSON is the text format most APIs use for data. It stores information as key and value pairs inside curly braces, and lists inside square brackets. It is easy for people to read and easy for programs to parse, which is why almost every

A lot of my automation work is really about reading JSON from one step and reshaping it for the next step. ## Connecting everyday tools I have worked with Google Sheets, Slack and Telegram in my workflows. Google Sheets can act as a simple database or a log of results. Slack and Telegram are useful for sending notifications or chatting with a bot. A small example of an idea: a workflow receives a message through a webhook, sends the text to an LLM through the OpenAI API, writes the result into a Google Sheet, and then notifies me on Telegram. ## AI inside automations The OpenAI API lets a workflow use a language model as one of its steps. Prompt engineering is what makes that step reliable: I give the model a clear role, clear instructions and a clear output format. # Student Help Desk: Long-Form Project Write-Up This is my own write-up of the Student Help Desk project, a RAG-based AI assistant for answering student queries. I wrote it to explain the idea, the way the pipeline works, and what I learned. ## The problem Students have lots of everyday questions. They want to know how a process works, where to find some information, or what a rule says. The answers usually exist somewhere in documents, but nobody enjoys searching through long files. A normal chatbot built only on a language model can sound confident while giving wrong answers, because it answers from what it learned during training and not from the real documents of the place the student belongs to. In AI this problem is called hallucination. ## The idea: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, fixes this by splitting the work into two jobs. First, a retrieval step looks through a custom knowledge base and finds the passages that are most relevant to the question. Second, a generation step gives those passages to the language model and asks it to write the answer using them. The model becomes more like a student taking an open-book exam than someone guessing from memory. ## How the pipeline works 1. **Collect the knowledge base.** I gathered the information students would need

it to write the answer using them. The model becomes more like a student taking an open-book exam than someone guessing from memory. ## How the pipeline works 1. **Collect the knowledge base.** I gathered the information students would need into a custom knowledge base made of text documents. 2. **Chunk the documents.** Long documents are cut into smaller pieces so that each piece covers one idea. Small chunks are easier to match with a question and fit easily inside a prompt. 3. **Turn chunks into vectors.** Each chunk is converted into a list of numbers, called an embedding, that captures its meaning. Chunks with similar meanings end up close to each other. 4. **Retrieve.** When a student asks a question, the question is converted into a vector too, and the system finds the chunks that are closest in meaning. This is the vector-based retrieval part of the project. 5. **Generate.** The best chunks and the question are sent to the LLM with instructions to answer from the given context. The answer comes back in natural language. ## Why I used vector-based retrieval Students never phrase a question the same way the document is written. Someone might ask "how do I get my marks rechecked" while the document says "re-evaluation request". A pure keyword search could miss this, because the

used vector-based retrieval Students never phrase a question the same way the document is written. Someone might ask "how do I get my marks rechecked" while the document says "re-evaluation request". A pure keyword search could miss this, because the words do not match. Vector retrieval looks at meaning, so it can connect the two sentences even without shared words. This is the main reason a vector-based retrieval pipeline improved the relevance of responses in my project. ## Reducing hallucinations The assistant is designed to rely on the retrieved context. The more clearly the prompt tells the model to answer only from the context, and to admit when the context does not contain the answer, the fewer made-up answers appear. Good chunking and good retrieval matter just as much as the prompt, because if the wrong passage is retrieved, even a well-behaved model will give a weak answer. ## What I learned - Retrieval quality decides answer quality. If the right chunk is not found, the LLM cannot answer correctly. - Chunk size matters. Chunks that are too big mix many topics together, and chunks that are too small lose context. - Prompting is part of the engineering. Clear instructions such as "use only the context" make a visible difference. - Testing with real questions is the best way to find weak spots. I learned to try questions phrased in different ways, not just the obvious ones. - Documentation matters. Writing down how the pipeline works helped me understand it better and made it easier to explain to others. ## What I would improve If I continued working on Student Help Desk, I would combine keyword search with vector search, which is called hybrid retrieval, because exact terms like names and codes are sometimes better matched by keywords. I would also add a way to show the source of each answer, so students can check the original document themselves. This digital clone project actually uses exactly that hybrid idea.
